# Algebraic Structure of Three-Flavor Neutrino Oscillations in Constant-Density Matter: Cayley–Hamilton Evolution, DMP Resummation, and Closed-Form Uncertainty Propagation

Aaryan Chaulagain<sup>1</sup>, Anju Dhakal<sup>1</sup>, and Daya Nidhi Chhatkuli<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>

<sup>1</sup>_Department of Physics, Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus, Tribhuwan University, Nepal_

**Abstract**

For three-flavor neutrino oscillations in constant-density matter, the Cayley– Hamilton theorem forces the evolution operator into a quadratic polynomial in _H_f, with coefficients determined by the three real eigenvalues through a Vandermonde system we write out explicitly. The eigenvalues follow from Cardano’s trigonometric formula, recovering the Zaglauer–Schwarzer expressions. The Denton–Minakata– Parke (DMP) approximation achieves fractional accuracy better than 10<sup>-4</sup> because its 1-3 rotation is a resummation: it removes the near-degeneracy that makes the naive expansion diverge at \(\hat{A}\rightarrow 1\), replacing the unbounded \((1-\hat{A})^{-1}\) with an effective parameter \(\epsilon_0\lesssim 0.015\) bounded uniformly in energy. A density-matrix treatment with a Lindblad term handles open-system decoherence and wave-packet effects in the same language; matter-dressed coherence lengths satisfy \(L/L_\mathrm{coh}^{ij}\sim 10^{-3}\)-10<sup>-2</sup> for terrestrial baselines. The CP asymmetry \(\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}(\nu_\mu\rightarrow\nu_e)\) is split into genuine and matter-induced fake contributions. Closed-form Jacobians in the NuFIT 6.0 parameter basis feed Monte Carlo and linearized uncertainty-propagation schemes, the latter validated against a Feldman–Cousins profile-likelihood mapping near physical boundaries. The Denton–Parke NuFast-LBL algorithm [Phys. Rev. D **110**, 073005 (2024)] remains the tool of choice for production fits; the analytic expressions here supply what iterative solvers cannot—parameter continuity, transparent limits, and Jacobians in closed form.

**Keywords:** Neutrino oscillations, MSW effect, Perturbative resummation, su(3) structure, Density matrix, Wave-packet decoherence, CP violation, Uncertainty propagation, PMNS matrix.

## 1 Introduction

Neutrino flavor oscillation is now a precision measurement problem. The three mixing angles, two mass-squared differences, and the CP-violating phase \(\delta_\mathrm{CP}\) of the Pontecorvo- Maki-Nakagawa-Sakata (PMNS) matrix [1, 2, 3] have been determined by reactor and accelerator experiments over the past two decades--Daya Bay [7], RENO [8], Double Chooz [9], T2K [10], and NOvA [11], building on the discovery of atmospheric and solar flavor conversion at Super-Kamiokande [4] and SNO [5] and the reactor confirmation by KamLAND [6]. The next generation--DUNE [12], Hyper-Kamiokande (HK) [13], and JUNO [14]--aims to measure leptonic CP violation at the five-sigma level and to resolve the mass ordering and the \(\theta_{23}\) octant. At that precision the oscillation probability calculation is no longer an afterthought: for DUNE, matter effects from coherent forward scattering [18, 19] contribute 10-20% corrections to \(P_{\mu e}\), and a systematic error in treating them maps directly onto the inferred value of \(\delta_\mathrm{CP}\) [20, 53].

The tools for computing those corrections have matured considerably. Zaglauer and Schwarzer [21] gave the closed-form cubic eigenvalues decades ago. More recently the Denton-Minakata-Parke (DMP) approximation [47] reached fractional accuracy below 10<sup>-4</sup> with a single rotation, and the NuFast-LBL algorithm of Denton and Parke [44] brought the cost down to about \(0.1\mu\)s per evaluation, roughly fifty times faster than a full eigensystem solve. Modern analyses use Feldman-Cousins [54] or nested-sampling methods requiring O(10<sup>6</sup>)-O(10<sup>7</sup>) evaluations per fit, which has driven the sustained effort to produce fast, accurate analytic expressions catalogued by Barenboim, Denton, Parke, and Ternes [43]. A contemporaneous pedagogical overview of the three-flavor paradigm is given by Denton [17]; the present work differs in emphasizing the algebraic structure of the evolution operator, the resummation interpretation of the DMP rotation, and the closed-form Jacobian infrastructure for uncertainty propagation.

What is missing is not any single ingredient but a treatment that ties them together for a reader who already knows the field. Take the evolution operator. That _S(L_) is quadratic in _H_<sub>f</sub> follows at once from Cayley-Hamilton, yet the neutrino literature tends to leave this implicit, and the Vandermonde system that turns the three eigenvalues into the three polynomial coefficients is, as far as we have found, nowhere written out. The DMP rotation is another case. Everyone knows it tames the \(\hat{A}\rightarrow 1\) divergence; less often noted is _why_, namely that it acts as a resummation and produces an effective expansion parameter \(\epsilon_0\) that remains bounded at every energy. And the closed-form Jacobians one needs to push parameter uncertainties through the probabilities--tied to the NuFIT 6.0 covariance and cross-checked with Feldman-Cousins near the boundaries-- we have not seen collected in one place. These are the threads this paper pulls together, along the way giving a common density-matrix language for the wave-packet and open- system corrections.

The organization follows the physics. Sections 2 and 3 fix conventions and build the matter Hamiltonian; Sections 4 and 5 develop its group-theoretic and spectral structure, including the adjugate eigenvectors and the convergence of iterative refinement. The density-matrix formalism (Section 6) carries through to the perturbative expansion and its \(\hat{A}=1\) divergence (Section 7), the wave-packet corrections (Section 8), the MSW resonance and the sub-resonant T2K/HK regime (Section 9), and the resummation reading of DMP (Section 10). The remaining sections cover CP and T asymmetries (Section 11), the magic baseline (Section 12), uncertainty propagation (Section 13), analytic limiting-case checks (Section 14), and extensions (Section 15), before we conclude.

## 2 Notation and Physical Inputs

### 2.1 PMNS Parameterization

We adopt the Particle Data Group (PDG) conventions \[22\]. Flavor eigenstates \(|\nu_\alpha\rangle\), \(\alpha\in\{e,\mu,\tau\}\), and mass eigenstates \(|\nu_i\rangle\), \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\), are related by the unitary PMNS matrix _U_:

\(|\nu_\alpha\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^3U_{\alpha i}|\nu_i\rangle,UU^\dagger=U^\dagger U=\mathbf{1}.\) (1)

The standard decomposition is \(U=R_{23}\Gamma_\delta R_{13}\Gamma_\delta^\dagger R_{12}\), with _R<sub>ij</sub>_ a real rotation by \(\theta_{ij}\) and \(\Gamma_\delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,e^{i\delta_\mathrm{CP}})\). Explicitly, with \(c_{ij}\equiv\mathrm{cos}\theta_{ij}\) and \(s_{ij}\equiv\mathrm{sin}\theta_{ij}\),

\(U=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
c_{12}c_{13} & s_{12}c_{13} & s_{13}e^{-i\delta_\mathrm{CP}} \\
-s_{12}c_{23}-c_{12}s_{23}s_{13}e^{i\delta_\mathrm{CP}} & c_{12}c_{23}-s_{12}s_{23}s_{13}e^{i\delta_\mathrm{CP}} & s_{23}c_{13} \\
s_{12}s_{23}-c_{12}c_{23}s_{13}e^{i\delta_\mathrm{CP}} & -c_{12}s_{23}-s_{12}c_{23}s_{13}e^{i\delta_\mathrm{CP}} & c_{23}c_{13}
\end{array}\right).\) (2)

Majorana phases do not affect oscillation probabilities \[23\] and are omitted. The mass- squared differences are \(\Delta m_{21}^2\equiv m_2^2-m_1^2\), \(\Delta m_{31}^2\equiv m_3^2-m_1^2\), and \(\Delta m_{32}^2=\Delta m_{31}^2-\Delta m_{21}^2\). Normal ordering (NO) has \(\Delta m_{31}^2>0\). A useful combination is the electron-weighted splitting \[24, 25\]

\(\Delta m_{ee}^2\equiv c_{12}^2\Delta m_{31}^2+s_{12}^2\Delta m_{32}^2=\Delta m_{31}^2-s_{12}^2\Delta m_{21}^2,\) (3)

which appears in \(\nu_e\) disappearance and in the DMP scheme \[43, 47\].

### 2.3 Matter Configuration and Experimental Benchmarks

For the reference examples we adopt the average crust configuration along a 295km baseline: \(\rho=2.6\mathrm{g}\mathrm{c}\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), _Y<sub>e</sub>_=0.5, _m<sub>N</sub>_=0.939GeV, _L_=295km.  2 lists the experimental benchmarks. The Fermi constant is \(G_F=1.1663787\times 10^{-5}\mathrm{GeV}^{-2}\) and \(1\mathrm{km}=5.06773\times 10^9\mathrm{eV}^{-1}\).

#### DUNE baseline geology.

The 1300km DUNE chord from Fermilab to the Sanford Underground Research Facility reaches a maximum depth of ∼32km, within the upper continental crust and never approaching the mantle. Kelly and Parke \[53\] showed that a path-averaged constant density \(\rho\approx 2.84\mathrm{g}\mathrm{c}\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) reproduces the exact oscillation probability at the O(1%) level for both the shape and normalization of the profile along this chord, so that a single-layer constant-density treatment suffices and PREM profile layering is not required for DUNE. We adopt this throughout and do not repeat the argument elsewhere.

## 3 Effective Hamiltonian in Matter

### 3.1 Derivation from the Electroweak Lagrangian

Neutrinos propagating through ordinary matter experience an index-of-refraction effect from coherent forward scattering off ambient fermions. The charged-current contribution from \(\nu_e^-e^-\) exchange, in the zero-momentum-transfer limit, collapses to a local four- fermion operator; the coherent sum over the electron background yields the effective potential \[18\]

\(V_\mathrm{CC}=\sqrt{2}G_FN_e=\sqrt{2}G_F\frac{\rho Y_e}{m_N}.\) (5)

### 3.2 Flavor-Basis Hamiltonian and Schrödinger Equation

The matter-modified flavor Hamiltonian is

\(H_\mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2E}U\mathrm{diag}(0,\Delta m_{21}^2,\Delta m_{31}^2)U^\dagger+\mathrm{diag}(V_\mathrm{CC},0,0),\) (6)

after subtracting \(m_1^2/(2E)\cdot\mathbf{1}\). _H_<sub>f</sub> is Hermitian, and the flavor state satisfies \(id\left|\nu(x)\right\rangle/dx=H_\mathrm{f}\left|\nu(x)\right\rangle\). For constant density,

\(\left|\nu(L)\right\rangle=S(L)\left|\nu(0)\right\rangle,S(L)=\mathrm{exp}(-iH_\mathrm{f}L),\) (7)

with _S(L_) unitary, so \(\sum_\beta P_{\alpha\beta}(L)=1\).

### 3.3 Numerical Stability: Hermitian Symmetrization

In floating-point arithmetic, construction of _U_ introduces anti-Hermitian noise at O(10<sup>-16</sup>). Projecting onto the Hermitian subspace via \(H_\mathrm{f}\leftarrow\frac{1}{2}(H_\mathrm{f}+H_\mathrm{f}^\dagger)\) removes this noise without altering the physics; afterward unitarity violations in _S(L_) are suppressed below O(10<sup>-10</sup>).

## 4 SU(3) Structure and the Evolution Operator

### 4.1 Embedding in the Lie Algebra u(3)

_H_<sub>f</sub> is an element of \(\mathfrak{u}(3)=\mathfrak{u}(1)\oplus\mathfrak{su}(3)\), with the u(1) factor the trace and the su(3) factor the traceless part. Since the trace contributes only an overall phase to _S(L_),

\(H_\mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{Tr}H_\mathrm{f}}{3}\mathbf{1}+\tilde{H}_\mathrm{f},\mathrm{Tr}\tilde{H}_\mathrm{f}=0,\tilde{H}_\mathrm{f}\in\mathfrak{su}(3).\) (8)

The Gell-Mann matrices \(\{\lambda_a\}_{a=1}^8\) \[26\] give \(\tilde{H}_\mathrm{f}=\sum_ah_a\lambda_a/2\) with \(h_a=\mathrm{Tr}(H_\mathrm{f}\lambda_a)\) (Appendix C).

### 4.2 Invariants and the Characteristic Polynomial

With \(\Lambda\equiv 2EH_\mathrm{f}\) and invariants \(I_n=\mathrm{Tr}(H_\mathrm{f}^n)\), the characteristic equation is

\(\Lambda^3-I_1\Lambda^2+\frac{1}{2}(I_1^2-I_2)\Lambda-\frac{1}{6}(I_1^3-3I_1I_2+2I_3)=0.\) (9)

In terms of _a_=2_EV_<sub>CC</sub>,

\(A=I_1=\Delta m_{21}^2+\Delta m_{31}^2+a,\) (10)

\(B=\frac{1}{2}(I_1^2-I_2)=\Delta m_{21}^2\Delta m_{31}^2+a\big[\Delta m_{21}^2(1-|U_{e2}|^2)+\Delta m_{31}^2(1-|U_{e3}|^2)\big],\) (11)

\(C=\mathrm{det}(2EH_\mathrm{f})=a\Delta m_{21}^2\Delta m_{31}^2|U_{e1}|^2.\) (12)

These are the Le Verrier-Faddeev coefficients \[27\], computable without explicit matrix inversion.

### 4.3 Cayley-Hamilton Structure of the Evolution Operator

By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, _H_<sub>f</sub> satisfies its own characteristic polynomial, so any analytic function _f(H_<sub>f</sub>) is a polynomial of degree at most two,

\(f(H_\mathrm{f})=c_0\mathbf{1}+c_1H_\mathrm{f}+c_2H_\mathrm{f}^2,\) (13)

with \(f(\omega_i)=c_0+c_1\omega_i+c_2\omega_i^2\) for the three eigenvalues \(\omega_i\) of _H_<sub>f</sub> (energy units). These are related to the rescaled mass-squared eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) of \(\Lambda=2EH_\mathrm{f}\) used from Section 5 onward by \(\omega_i=\lambda_i/(2E)\). Applied to \(f(\omega)=e^{-i\omega L}\),<tbc>

\(S(L)=c_0(L)\mathbf{1}+c_1(L)H_\mathrm{f}+c_2(L)H_\mathrm{f}^2,\) (14)

<tbc>with the coefficients fixed by the Vandermonde system

\(\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
1 & \omega_1 & \omega_1^2 \\
1 & \omega_2 & \omega_2^2 \\
1 & \omega_3 & \omega_3^2
\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ c }
c_0 \\
c_1 \\
c_2
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{ c }
e^{-i\omega_1L} \\
e^{-i\omega_2L} \\
e^{-i\omega_3L}
\end{array}\right),\omega_i=\lambda_i/(2E).\) (15)

The three-flavor amplitude in constant-density matter is thus determined entirely by the three eigenvalues. While the Cayley-Hamilton property is implicit in the matrix- exponential literature, the explicit Vandermonde system (15) connecting eigenvalues to evolution-operator coefficients is not, to our knowledge, written out in this form in prior neutrino references.

## 5 Exact Hamiltonian Diagonalization

### 5.1 Exact Cubic Eigenvalue Solution

It is convenient to diagonalize the rescaled matrix \(\Lambda\equiv 2EH_\mathrm{f}\), whose coefficients _A_, _B_, _C_ (Eqs. 10-12) carry dimensions of mass-squared; we denote its eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) (units eV<sup>2</sup>), so that in vacuum \(\lambda_i\rightarrow m_i^2-m_1^2\) and the eigenvalue differences reduce to \(\Delta\lambda_{ij}\rightarrow\Delta m_{ij}^2\). The physical phase entering the evolution operator and the oscillation probabilities is \(\lambda_iL/(2E)\); accordingly the oscillation probabilities of Section 5.4 are written with the combination \(\Delta\lambda_{ij}/(2E)\), which is dimensionally an inverse length. Substituting \(\lambda=\mu+A/3\) gives the depressed cubic \(\mu^3+p\mu+q=0\) with _p=B-A_<sup>2</sup>/3 and _q_=-2_A_<sup>3</sup>/27+_AB/_3-_C_. Since \(\Lambda\) is Hermitian, all roots are real, the discriminant \(\Delta_\mathrm{cubic}=-4p^3-27q^2\ge 0\), and _p\<_0. The three real roots follow from Cardano’s trigonometric method \[20, 56\],

\(\lambda_k=\frac{A}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{A^2-3B}\mathrm{cos}\left(\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{arccos}\left(\frac{2A^3-9AB+27C}{2(A^2-3B)^{3/2}}\right)-\frac{2\pi k}{3}\right),k=0,1,2,\) (16)

the Zaglauer-Schwarzer result \[21\]. The cosine (not hyperbolic) form is the correct branch for a Hermitian matrix with three real roots.

### 5.2 DMP Approximation and Its Accuracy

Defining \(x\equiv a/\Delta m_{ee}^2\), DMP \[47\] approximate the largest eigenvalue by

\(\lambda_3\approx\Delta m_{31}^2+\frac{\Delta m_{ee}^2}{2}\left(x-1+\sqrt{(1-x)^2+4xs_{13}^2}\right).\) (17)

The fractional accuracy relative to the exact eigenvalues is better than 10<sup>-4</sup> for terrestrial energies and both orderings \[43, 44\], as in  3. A single Newton-Raphson correction,

\(\lambda_3\rightarrow\lambda_3-\frac{X(\lambda_3)}{X'(\lambda_3)},X(\lambda)=\lambda^3-A\lambda^2+B\lambda-C,\) (18)

improves the fractional precision by several orders of magnitude \[44\].

## 5.3 Eigenvectors via the Adjugate Method

Once the eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) are known, the squared elements of the eigenvector matrix _V<sub>e</sub>_ follow from the adjugate of \((\lambda I-H_\mathrm{f})\), as developed by Abdullahi and Parke \[27\]:

\(|V_{e\alpha i}|^2=\frac{\lambda_i^2-S_{\alpha\alpha}\lambda_i+T_{\alpha\alpha}}{\Delta\lambda_{ij}\Delta\lambda_{ik}},\) (19)

where \(j,k\neq i\) and

\(S_{\alpha\alpha}=A-(2E)H_{f\alpha\alpha},\) (20)

\(T_{\alpha\alpha}=(2E)^2[\mathrm{Adj}(H_\mathrm{f})]_{\alpha\alpha}.\) (21)

The numerator quantities \(S_{\alpha\alpha}\) and \(T_{\alpha\alpha}\) are the diagonal elements of the adjugate of (2_EH_<sub>f</sub>); Eq. (19) is thus the adjugate formula of \[27\]. The closely related eigenvector- eigenvalue identity of Denton, Parke, Tao, and Zhang \[28\] expresses the same moduli through products of eigenvalue differences for sub-matrices; we use the adjugate form because Adj(_H_<sub>f</sub>) is already available from the Le Verrier-Faddeev coefficients of Section 4.2.

### Denominator protection. The denominators \(\Delta\lambda_{ij}\Delta\lambda_{ik}\) become small near the atmospheric resonance (\(\hat{A}\rightarrow 1\)). ## 8 Wave-Packet Decoherence Corrections

### 8.1 Framework and Coherence Lengths

Physical neutrinos are produced and detected as wave-packets of finite spatial extent \[35, 36, 37\]. Different mass eigenstates propagate with different group velocities and separate after the coherence length \[39, 40, 41\]. A Gaussian model \[38, 42\] assigns a production position uncertainty \(\sigma_x\sim 10^{-15}\)-10<sup>-13</sup>m. In constant-density matter the coherence length for the pair (_i,j_) is \[39\]

\(L_\mathrm{coh}^{ij}=\frac{4\sqrt{2}E^2\sigma_x}{|\Delta\lambda_{ij}|},\) (42)

where \(\Delta\lambda_{ij}\) is the matter-dressed mass-squared splitting (the eigenvalue difference of \(\Lambda=2EH_\mathrm{f}\)); in vacuum \(\Delta\lambda_{ij}\rightarrow\Delta m_{ij}^2\) and this reduces to the familiar form \(L_\mathrm{coh}^{ij}=4\sqrt{2}E^2\sigma_x/|\Delta m_{ij}^2|\). For the 31-pair at _E_=0.6GeV, with \(\sigma_x\sim 10^{-13}\)m and \(\Delta m_{31}^2\approx 2.5\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{eV}^2\),

\(L_\mathrm{coh}^{31}=\frac{4\sqrt{2}\left(0.6\mathrm{GeV}\right)^2\left(10^{-13}\mathrm{m}\right)}{2.5\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{eV}^2}\approx 8\times 10^4\mathrm{km},\) (43)

two to three orders of magnitude larger than the T2K/HK baseline. Decoherence is therefore negligible for terrestrial long-baseline experiments, but only by a factor \(L/L_\mathrm{coh}^{31}\sim 10^{-3}\)-10<sup>-2</sup> ( 5)--not the much larger margin sometimes quoted. Solar neutrinos are the exception: \(L/L_\mathrm{coh}\gg 1\), coherences wash out, and the survival probability reduces to the incoherent sum \(P_{ee}^\mathrm{solar}=\sum_i|U_{ei}|^2|V_{eei}|^2\) in the adiabatic MSW picture \[19, 59\].

## 10 Resummation Interpretation of the DMP Rotation

### 10.1 Origin of the Divergence

The divergence near \(\hat{A}\rightarrow 1\) arises because the unperturbed Hamiltonian (at \(\alpha=0\)) has eigenvalues _V_<sub>CC</sub> and \(\Delta m_{31}^2/(2E)\) that become degenerate at \(\hat{A}=1\); the perturbative denominator \(\Delta\lambda_{13}^{(0)}\sim(1-\hat{A})\Delta m_{31}^2/(2E)\) then vanishes.

### 10.2 DMP Rotation as a Resummation

The DMP procedure \[47\] first performs an exact rotation in the 13-sector by \(\theta_{13}^M\), \(H_e=R_{13}^{-1}(\theta_{13}^M)H_\mathrm{f}R_{13}(\theta_{13}^M)\), after which the 13-sector off-diagonals vanish exactly. The remaining expansion parameter is \[47, 43\]

\(\epsilon_0=\frac{\Delta m_{21}^2}{\Delta m_{ee}^2}sin(\theta_{13}^M-\theta_{13})s_{12}c_{12},|\epsilon_0|\le\frac{\Delta m_{21}^2}{\Delta m_{ee}^2}s_{12}c_{12}\lesssim 0.015,\) (46)

where the upper bound follows from \(|sin(\theta_{13}^M-\theta_{13})|\le 1\) and is reached only near the atmospheric resonance. The key point is that \(\epsilon_0\) is bounded uniformly in \(\hat{A}\): the resonant denominator that was unbounded in the naive expansion is absorbed into the matter rotation angle \(\theta_{13}^M\), leaving a finite expansion parameter at all energies. The series \(P_{\mu e}^\mathrm{DMP}=P_{\mu e}^{(0)}+\epsilon_0P_{\mu e}^{(1)}+\epsilon_0^2P_{\mu e}^{(2)}+\cdots\) therefore converges uniformly in energy. The original DMP papers \[47, 43\] demonstrate the 10<sup>-4</sup> accuracy numerically; the complementary question of rotations versus perturbative expansions is analysed in detail by Denton, Parke, and Zhang \[48\]. What the present framing adds is the reason why this accuracy follows from first principles: the DMP rotation is a degenerate-eigenvalue resummation, in which the troublesome \((1-\hat{A})^{-1}\) is absorbed into \(\theta_{13}^M\) and replaced by the bounded \(\epsilon_0\).

## 11 CP Violation: Analytic Structure in Matter

### 11.1 CP Asymmetry and Its Decomposition

The appearance-channel CP asymmetry is \(\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}\equiv P(\nu_\mu\rightarrow\nu_e)-P(\bar{\nu}_\mu\rightarrow\bar{\nu}_e)\). Using \(\mathrm{Im}[V_{e\beta i}V_{e\alpha i}^*V_{e\beta j}^*V_{e\alpha j}]=+J_\mathrm{mat}\) for \((i,j)\in\{(2,1),(3,2),(1,3)\}\) and -_J_<sub>mat</sub> otherwise, together with a trigonometric product identity,

\(\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}^\mathrm{genuine}=-16J_\mathrm{mat}\mathrm{sin}\frac{\Delta\lambda_{21}L}{4E}\mathrm{sin}\frac{\Delta\lambda_{31}L}{4E}\mathrm{sin}\frac{\Delta\lambda_{32}L}{4E}.\) (47)

### 11.2 Genuine vs. Fake CP Violation

The total asymmetry splits as \[57, 58\] \(\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}^\mathrm{total}=\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}^\mathrm{genuine}+\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}^\mathrm{fake}\), where the genuine term is odd under \(J\rightarrow-J\) and vanishes at _J_=0, while

\(\mathcal{A}_\mathrm{CP}^\mathrm{fake}\approx 4s_{23}^2s_{13}^2c_{13}^2\frac{\mathrm{sin}^2[(1-\hat{A})\Delta]}{(1-\hat{A})^2}-4s_{23}^2s_{13}^2c_{13}^2\frac{\mathrm{sin}^2[(1+\hat{A})\Delta]}{(1+\hat{A})^2}\) (48)

is odd in \(\hat{A}\) and survives even at \(\delta_\mathrm{CP}=0\). For strictly uniform matter, a non-zero T-asymmetry \(\mathcal{A}_T\equiv P(\nu_\mu\rightarrow\nu_e)-P(\nu_e\rightarrow\nu_\mu)\) is a clean signature of fundamental T-violation \[63\], free from the fake asymmetry.

### 13.3 Boundary Caveat and Feldman-Cousins Validation

Wilks’ theorem is routinely violated in oscillation analyses due to physical boundaries, the cyclic variable \(\delta_\mathrm{CP}\in[0,2\pi)\), and discrete degeneracies. The Gaussian Jacobian linearization can produce unphysical negative probability excursions near \(\theta_{13}\rightarrow 0\) and near the cyclic boundary \(\delta_\mathrm{CP}\rightarrow 0\equiv 2\pi\). All Jacobian-based bands reported here are therefore validated against a Feldman-Cousins unified profile-likelihood mapping \[54\] before use in fits. Parameter correlations enter through the off-diagonal terms of the covariance matrix,

\(\mathrm{Var}[P]=\underbrace{\sum_iJ_i^2\sigma_i^2}_\text{diagonal}+2\underbrace{\sum_{i<j}J_iJ_j\Sigma_{ij}}_\text{correlation},\) (57)

so a diagonal-only error budget systematically misestimates the band width whenever the global fit reports non-negligible off-diagonal \(\Sigma_{ij}\). When the full covariance is available-- for example from a joint experimental likelihood, or from the public \(\chi^2\) profiles of the global fit \[15, 16\]--it should be propagated directly through Eq. (57); the closed-form Jacobian (Section 13.2) makes this a single matrix product.

## 14 Analytic Validation Against Limiting Cases

### Vacuum limit (\(\hat{A}\rightarrow 0\)).

By L’Hôpital’s rule \(\mathrm{sin}(\hat{A}\Delta)/\hat{A}\rightarrow\Delta\), \(\mathrm{sin}[(1-\hat{A})\Delta]/(1-\hat{A})\rightarrow\mathrm{sin}\Delta\), and \(\mathrm{sin}^2[(1-\hat{A})\Delta]/(1-\hat{A})^2\rightarrow\mathrm{sin}^2\Delta\), recovering

\(P_{\mu e}^\mathrm{vac}=4s_{23}^2s_{13}^2c_{13}^2\mathrm{sin}^2\Delta+8\alpha J_\mathrm{CP}\mathrm{cos}(\Delta+\delta_\mathrm{CP})\Delta\mathrm{sin}\Delta+4\alpha^2c_{13}^2c_{23}^2s_{12}^2c_{12}^2\Delta^2+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^3).\) (58)

### High-energy limit.

For \(E\rightarrow\infty\) at fixed _L,V_<sub>CC</sub>, \(\hat{A}\rightarrow\infty\), \(H_\mathrm{f}\rightarrow\mathrm{diag}(V_\mathrm{CC},0,0)\), and all three terms vanish: \(T_\mathrm{atm}\propto\hat{A}^{-2}\), \(T_\mathrm{int}\propto\hat{A}^{-1}\), \(T_\mathrm{sol}\propto\hat{A}^{-2}\).

#### Two-flavor limit.

Setting \(\theta_{12}=0\) (\(\alpha\rightarrow 0\) in _T_int_,T_sol), \(P_{\mu e}\rightarrow 4s_{23}^2s_{13}^2c_{13}^2sin^2[(1-\hat{A})\Delta]/(1-\hat{A})^2\), the two-flavor MSW appearance formula. Unitarity \(\sum_\beta P_{\alpha\beta}=1\) holds algebraically for the exact solver and to \(\mathcal{O}(\alpha^3)\) for the perturbative expressions.

## 15 Extensions and Positioning

### 15.1 Positioning Relative to NuFast-LBL

The NuFast-LBL algorithm \[44\] runs at \(\sim 0.1\mu\)s per evaluation, with fractional precision \(\le 10^{-4}\) at zeroth order and \(\le 10^{-9}\) with a single Newton–Raphson step, surpassing full eigensystem computations by \(\sim 50\times\). The exact and perturbative expressions in this paper are positioned strictly as _exact theoretical anchors_: they provide analytic continuity in all six parameters, closed-form Jacobians (Section 13.2), transparent algebraic limiting cases (Section 14), and the explicit resummation structure (Section 10)--capabilities iterative solvers do not provide by construction. For production Monte Carlo analyses requiring O(10<sup>6</sup>)-O(10<sup>7</sup>) evaluations, NuFast-LBL is the recommended tool.

### 15.2 Constant-Density Validity and Longer Baselines

As noted in Section 2.3, the path-averaged constant density reproduces the exact DUNE probability to O(1%) \[53\], with no residual profile-shape sensitivity at DUNE’s expected precision. For longer baselines (\(L\unknown 5000\)km) where the chord samples upper-mantle material, a piecewise-layer treatment \(S_\text{total}=\prod_ke^{-iH_f(\rho_k)L_k}\) is required.

### 15.3 Parameter Degeneracies, NSI, and Sterile States

The appearance probability is invariant at leading order under \[60\] \(\delta_\text{CP}\rightarrow\pi-\delta_\text{CP}\), \(\theta_{23}\rightarrow\pi/2-\theta_{23}\); this degeneracy is lifted at \(\mathcal{O}(\alpha^2)\) by \(T_\text{sol}\propto c_{23}^2\). The density-matrix formalism accommodates non-standard interactions through an upgraded matter potential \[18, 64\], \(V_\text{mat}^\text{NSI}=\sqrt{2}G_FN_e(\mathbf{1}+\unknown)\), with \(\unknown\) the NSI matrix now constrained by COHERENT \[66, 67\]; the LMA-Dark degeneracy \[65\] requires \(\epsilon_{ee}\approx-2\). For a sterile state \[68, 69, 70\], the PMNS matrix becomes \(4\times 4\) and the Cayley–Hamilton polynomial for _S(L_) rises to cubic order, \(S(L)=c_0\mathbf{1}+c_1H_\text{f}+c_2H_\text{f}^2+c_3H_\text{f}^3\), with a quartic characteristic equation solvable by Ferrari’s method \[71\]; the algebraic logic of Sections 4-5 carries over directly.

### 15.4 Future Landscape

DUNE Phase II targets \(5\sigma\) CP sensitivity over more than 75% of \(\delta_\text{CP}\) values \[12\]; HK \[13\] adds complementary _L/E_ coverage; JUNO will fix \(\Delta m_{31}^2\) to 0.3% \[14\]; and IceCube- Gen2 \[77\] and KM3NeT/ORCA will probe the ordering via Earth matter effects. The algorithmic frontier continues to move toward more complex propagation scenarios beyond the constant-density LBL setting of this work.

## 16 Conclusion

None of the individual results here is new in isolation; the value lies in how they fit together. The starting point is the Cayley–Hamilton structure of _S(L_). Any analytic<tbc>

function of a \(3\times 3\) matrix is a quadratic polynomial in it (Eq. 13), so the evolution operator in constant-density matter is fixed once the three eigenvalues are known, and the Vandermonde system (Eq. 15) is nothing more than the bookkeeping that makes this concrete. From there the DMP rotation reads naturally as a resummation rather than an approximation: it eliminates the near-degenerate eigenvalue behind the \(\hat{A}\rightarrow 1\) divergence and replaces the unbounded \((1-\hat{A})^{-1}\) with the bounded \(\epsilon_0\le 0.015\) (Eq. 46). The same operator language carries the wave-packet analysis, which puts the matter- dressed coherence lengths in the 10<sup>4</sup>-10<sup>6</sup>km range and hence _L/L_<sub>coh</sub> at the 10<sup>-3</sup>-10<sup>-2</sup> level--decoherence is small, though by a more modest margin than is sometimes assumed. Finally, the closed-form Jacobians in the NuFIT 6.0 basis (Eqs. 51-56) make linearized uncertainty propagation a matter of one matrix product, with Feldman-Cousins held in reserve for the boundaries where the Gaussian picture breaks.

We are not proposing a replacement for NuFast-LBL. For the O(10<sup>6</sup>)-O(10<sup>7</sup>) evaluations a production fit demands, the Denton-Parke algorithm [44] is the right choice and we say so plainly. The analytic route earns its place elsewhere: where one wants continuity in every parameter, limits that can be read off by hand, and Jacobians that propagate correlated uncertainties in closed form. Those are the demands of interpretation and validation, not of likelihood minimization, and that is the work this framework is meant for.

The extensions to non-standard interactions and sterile-neutrino su(4) topologies follow the same algebraic logic, with the Cayley-Hamilton polynomial rising to cubic order for the \(4\times 4\) case. As DUNE, HK, and JUNO approach their design sensitivities, the interplay between matter effects, CP violation, and parameter degeneracies will require exactly the kind of algebraic transparency this framework is designed to provide.
